extracted.intended_audience: scientists and educated readers interested in climatology, meteorology, and physical geography
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive and explanatory exposition of atmospheric composition, the principal features of the atmosphere, and the climatic factors (isothermal/isotheral/isochimenal lines, winds, humidity, electric state) that determine climate and vegetation limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of dry air
rubrics_metrics.description: A volume of dry air contains 20.8 of oxygen, and 79.2 of nitrogen, besides from two to five thousandth parts of carbonic acid gas, a still smaller quantity of carbureted hydrogen gas, and traces of ammoniacal vapors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References to Dumas, Boussingault, Saussure, and Liebig; footnotes provide measured proportions and local variations (e.g., Audilly CO2 proportion 0.00028–0.00031).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local and seasonal variation of oxygen
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations (Lewy) render it probable that the quantity of oxygen varies perceptibly but slightly over the sea and in the interior of continents, according to local conditions or to the seasons of the year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes in oxygen dissolved in the sea produced by microscopic animal organisms may alter the strata of air in immediate contact with it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of atmospheric carbonic acid (CO2)
rubrics_metrics.description: CO2 is supplied by respiration of animals (who receive carbon from vegetable food), from the interior of the earth near exhausted volcanoes and thermal springs, from decomposition of carbureted hydrogen gas in the atmosphere, and from electric discharges of clouds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plant nocturnal exhalation of CO2 is not counted here because it is counter-balanced by daytime photosynthesis; see citations to Boussingault and Liebig.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of noxious accidental admixtures (miasmata)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accidentally mixed substances near the ground (miasmatic and gaseous contagia) may exercise a noxious influence on animal organization; their chemical nature not yet ascertained by direct analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inferred from decay processes and pathology; possible constituents include ammoniacal vapors, sulphureted hydrogen, and polybasic ternary and quaternary compounds; may generate ague and typhus fever in various forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particulate and biological dust in the atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Winds and currents caused by ground heating can carry solid substances reduced to a fine powder to considerable elevation; dust (e.g., to Cape Verd Islands) contains silicious-shelled infusoria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ehrenberg's discovery cited; fogs with peculiar smells also indicate lower-strata admixtures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal features of a descriptive picture of the atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerated principal features: (1) Variations of atmospheric pressure; (2) Climatic distribution of heat; (3) Distribution of the humidity of the atmosphere; (4) The electric condition of the atmosphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each head encompasses many subordinate phenomena (e.g., horary oscillations, isothermal lines, precipitation forms, cloud electricity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Variations of atmospheric pressure (horary oscillations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Horary oscillations occur with regularity (especially in the tropics) producing an ebb and flow in the atmosphere; these differ by geographic latitude, season, and elevation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bouvard and others' calculations show lunar attraction accounts for only a tiny fraction; diurnal oscillations can be regular enough to ascertain the hour within 15–17 minutes in some regions; observations on mountains need many data for trustworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climatic distribution of heat
rubrics_metrics.description: Distribution of heat depends on relative positions of transparent and opaque surface masses (fluid vs. solid) and hypsometrical configuration of continents; these determine isothermal line position and curvature horizontally and vertically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of isothermal, isotheral, and isochimenal lines for comparative climatology; differences between annual/summer/winter mean temperatures are important for agricultural and vegetational implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of atmospheric humidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative relations of humidity depend on differences in solid and oceanic surfaces, distance from the equator and level of the sea, the form in which aqueous vapor is precipitated, and connection between these deposits and temperature changes and wind directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humidity distribution affects climatic character and precipitation forms; interactions with temperature and wind are emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electric condition of the atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider relation of ascending vapors to electric charge and cloud form, their daily and seasonal variation, differences between cold and warm zones, frequency and periodicity of thunderstorms, formation in summer/winter, and causal connection with hail and water/sand spouts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary cause of the serene-sky electric condition remains contested; linkages to cloud physics and meteorological extremes are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isobarometric and isobarometric-windrose analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Connecting places by 'isobarometric' lines (equal mean difference between monthly extremes of the barometer) yields curves that indicate influence of land form and sea distribution on atmospheric oscillations; 'barometric windroses' (tables of pressure during different winds) afford deeper insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps relate prevailing winds and regional pressure variability to geographic features; examples include Hindostan, Antilles, Western Europe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of rotation and opposing upper currents
rubrics_metrics.description: Difference of temperature between equatorial and polar regions engenders two opposite currents; owing to rotational velocity differences, polar current is deflected eastward and equatorial westward, and their opposition controls major phenomena (pressure, cloud formation, winds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dove's 'law of rotation' explains many meteorological processes and cloud forms; points to where upper currents descend and interact with surface processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of long-distance and long-duration observations (magnetic stations)
rubrics_metrics.description: A long chain of 'magnetic stations' and comparison of observations made at places many hundred miles apart are essential to determine the 'law of the winds' and to learn the origin ('whence') of aerial currents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes necessity of sustained (>20 years where possible) and geographically distributed observations to decide whether currents originate at ends or in the middle of station series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isothermal, isotheral, and isochimenal lines for comparative climatology
rubrics_metrics.description: Lines of equal mean annual temperature (isothermal), equal winter (isochimenal), and equal summer (isotheral) should be connected and examined; differences among these lines are crucial to understanding regional climate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humboldt introduced these lines; they are expected to be gradually perfected by investigators and serve as foundations for comparative climatology, analogous to graphic systems used in terrestrial magnetism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'climate' as a compound of factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Climate (in general sense) indicates all atmospheric changes that sensibly affect organisms: temperature, humidity, barometrical pressure variations, calm/contrary winds, electric tension, atmospheric purity/noxious admixtures, and degree of transparency/clearness of the sky.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All these affect radiation, plant development, fruit ripening, and human feelings and mental condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes that raise mean temperature
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors tending to 'raise' temperature include proximity of a western coast in temperate zone; divided continental configuration into peninsulas and bays; position relative to polar ice or tropical continental masses; prevailing southerly/westerly winds; mountain chains acting as protective walls; infrequency of swamps; absence of woods in dry sandy soil; constant summer serenity of the sky; and vicinity of warm oceanic currents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These causes modify isothermal line inflections and are to be considered when explaining local temperature increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes that lower mean temperature
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors tending to 'lower' temperature include elevation above sea-level (when not part of an extended plain); vicinity of an eastern coast in high/middle latitudes; compact continental configuration without indentations; extension toward polar ice without open winter sea; absence of tropical continental land within same meridian; mountain chains impeding warm winds; isolated peaks producing cold descending currents; extensive woods increasing evaporation/radiation cooling; frequent swamps; cloudy summers; and very clear winter skies favoring radiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These disturbing causes act in combination to produce concave inflections of isothermal lines and must be separately considered before combining effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method: separate and then combine disturbing causes
rubrics_metrics.description: To understand isothermal line inflections, distinguish between different orders of disturbing causes, consider each separately, and then investigate their total effect (motion, local curvature) and mutual dependence to potentially derive empirical, numerically expressed laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggests a systematic empirical approach to connect isolated facts into general laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade winds and their effect on temperate zone winds
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade winds (easterly in tropics) give rise, in temperate zones, to west or west-southwest winds; east winds of the continent are cooler than west winds when not influenced by oceanic currents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains hemispheric and coastal temperature contrasts and references historical observers (Forster) and later meteorologists (Dove, Kämtz).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insular/littoral versus continental climate contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Sea moderates temperatures producing milder winters and cooler summers (insular/littoral climates), while interior of continents exhibit 'excessive' climates with large seasonal temperature ranges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: interior Asiatic towns have summer heat similar to Berlin but much colder winters; western coasts (e.g., Europe) show milder winters and greater maritime moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of comparing mean annual, summer, and winter temperatures for agricultural implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions like 'how many degrees colder is America than Europe?' are meaningless without specific parallel-by-parallel comparisons; separate differences exist for each parallel and special comparison of winter/summer temperatures is needed to judge agricultural/comfort influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives numerical examples comparing Nain, Gottenburg, Halifax, Bordeaux, New York, Naples, St. Augustine, and Cairo to show varying differences by latitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between direct and diffused light affecting vegetation
rubrics_metrics.description: Difference between direct and diffused light (clear vs overcast skies) influences local, 'unmeasured' heat developed in the living vegetable cell and affects ripeness of fruits and success of cultivation even when thermometric readings in shade are similar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humboldt urges physicists and physiologists to attend to this difference; examples explain why similar shade-temperatures can yield different plant outcomes (Cherbourg vs inland vineyards).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thermic scale of cultivation and specific thermal requirements (vine example)
rubrics_metrics.description: When forming a thermic scale of cultivations (vanilla, cacao, banana... to vines), geographical limits of cultivation show other climatic relations besides mean annual temperature are involved. For vine cultivation to procure 'potable' wine it is 'requisite that the mean annual heat should exceed 49 degrees, that the winter temperature upward of 64 degrees.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A table of mean year/winter/spring/summer/autumn temperatures for European places (Bordeaux, Strasbourg, Berlin, Cherbourg, Dublin etc.) is cited to illustrate how similar mean temperatures can result in different viticultural outcomes due to sunshine and seasonal distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of long-series meteorological observations and defined seasonal conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliable climatological conclusions depend on sufficiently long series of observations (examples use 10–35 years in table) and consistent seasonal definitions (December–February as winter months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table of observation-years accompanies temperature data; the influence of late May frosts and timing of ripening are emphasized as agriculturally significant.
